sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Standardization**: Sher Shah replaced the mixed-metal and debased coins of the Lodi/Sultanate era with a **tri-metallic system** (Gold, Silver, Copper).
• **Weight Uniformity**: He established fixed weights for coins, specifically the **Rupiya** (Silver) at 178 grains and the **Dam** (Copper) at 320 grains.
• **Administrative Integration**: Coinage was used as a tool for **fiscal centralization**, ensuring that taxes could be paid in the new standardized currency, thereby reducing exchange rate volatility.
• **Key Metric**: The ratio between the Silver Rupiya and Copper Dam was fixed at **1:40**, providing a stable exchange mechanism for trade.

items.definition: The simultaneous use of Gold, Silver, and Copper coins. It provided a hierarchy of currency for different levels of economic activity.
Sher Shah established multiple mints across the empire to ensure uniform supply and prevent counterfeiting through strict state supervision.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Economic Integration**: Standardized currency facilitated the 'Grand Trunk Road' trade, linking Bengal to the Indus.
• **Fiscal Policy**: Taxes (Mal) were collected in the new currency, forcing peasants to sell produce in markets, boosting monetization.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Resistance from local money changers (Sarrafs) and the difficulty of maintaining purity in remote provinces.
• **Legacy**: The Rupiya remained the standard currency throughout the Mughal period and was adopted by the British East India Company.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'R-D-A' (Rupiya, Dam, Ashrafi).
• **Decoded Meaning**: R (Silver/Rupiya), D (Copper/Dam), A (Gold/Ashrafi). Remember: Silver is the 'King' of the system (178 grains).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often claims Sher Shah 'invented' the Rupee. Clarify: He 'standardized' and 'popularized' it; the term 'Rupiya' existed earlier but was not a standard unit.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Monetary Integration' to describe how Sher Shah's coinage acted as a precursor to the modern Indian fiscal union.

keyTakeaways: Sher Shah Suri's tri-metallic system formed the backbone of the Mughal and British Indian currency.
The 1:40 ratio between Silver Rupiya and Copper Dam was the key to market stability.
His reforms were driven by the need for administrative centralization and trade facilitation.
